Although {{AbstractPollingChannel.receive()}} is blocking, we never use it in test cases (and if there are any such remaining tests in SI, they need to be fixed). The problem is that a bug in a test can hang the CI build server. It is better to receive with a looong timeout so at least the build can fail rather than hang. In most cases, in SI we use {{receive(10000)}} but the general rule of thumb is to wait at least 10x the expected timeout or 10 seconds, whichever is the larger.

`receive(10000)` doesn't mean it will wait 10 seconds; it will wait up to 10 seconds before failing. This can be hidden within the test fixture. In my experience, using external rules is too brittle; tests themselves know what a reasonable time to wait is.

Given a passive component, say a processor (filter), attach it to a tap that's a fire hose. This is only a problem when a stream starts with a {{tap}} because with a "normal" stream, the last module to be bound is the source, and we don't start it until the source itself is bound; hence no messages flow to the downstream processors. These channels remain in the context when both the producer and consumer are undeployed. It's rather benign in that the channels will be reused if the modules are redeployed, but it is a leak and should be address

When producers are created/bound dynamically (e.g. from the router sink), they are not unbound when the module is undeployed. There is currently no metadata in the binding to provide that functionality. It is not critical because the producers are just sitting there (and may be reused if the module is redeployed, but it is a leak and should be addressed at some time.

Inside the cppsuite framework, there are numerous ways where we can rollback the current active transaction. The functions {{cancommit}}, {{insert}} or {{update}} checks if the current test needs to rollback. If so, we return back false, and the test needs to perform a rollback. The function {{commit}} performs WiredTiger's committransaction(), if the function call fails, internally WT performs a rollback. It is possible that a particular test can be stuck when rollbacks are continuously called.

This ticket came out of an issue we saw with logkeeper, where the checkpoint cleanup was causing long checkpoints and stalls. [~agorrod], [~haribabu.kommi] and I identified areas of improvements, which are as follows: Limit the amount of I/O generated by the history cleanup for checkpoints. This could be done by spreading the work across the checkpoints, instead of walking the whole tree each checkpoint. Potentially we could save the location of the walk and resume at the next checkpoint. The in

Following possible solutions can improve the checkpoint cleanup: Do not urgently evict the pages that are read by the checkpoint process, they should go through the normal eviction cycle by removing the WTREADWONTNEED flag for all the reads by the checkpoint. Track the number of pages that are loaded for each btree and limit them to a configured number of pages and in the next checkpoint resume it from the location where it was stopped earlier.

There is another modification to importantly consider here and that is that any shutdown should not check for obsolete pages, not just shutdown with timestamps. There are code paths in MongoDB that use {{conn->close(conn, "usetimestamp=false")}} and when that is in use it has been seen to take hours to shutdown. Almost certainly the reason is that the code here in {{btsync.c:wtsyncfile}}: {noformat} if (btree->type == BTREEROW) internalcleanup = !FISSET(conn, WTCONNRECOVERING | WTCONNCLOSINGTIME

To add more context, MongoDB is seeing some customers, when they do a clean shutdown with {{usetimestamp=false}} take hours to shutdown. Running {{strace}} shows the system is doing massive amounts of reading, 20x to writes during the shutdown. MongoDB has a legitimate use case for using that configuration for closing.
[~daniel.gottlieb] suggested, for the MongoDB use case, to consider a configuration setting for close to skip the checkpoint cleanup (assuming that is safe).

The existence of previous run transaction ids on the page image leads to wrong transaction visibility as WT restarts the transaction ids upon start and the oplog replay happens using a transaction id that is lower than the transaction ids on the page. This is a regression introduced in MongoDB 4.4.5 with WT-6673 change of resetting the transaction id's present on the page until the rollback to stable is finished as part of recovery.

Implemented the solution to have all the disk images that are prepared with a {{write generation number}} instead of updating the write generation only when it is writing to disk. During normal execution, Checkpoint flushed a page image to disk containing transaction id's and some of the key updates written to the page are more than the stable timestamp. 2. The implementation of random cursors on tiered tables – i.e., {{curtierednextrandom()}} – can be pretty skewed. We should come up with a better way to select random items. In the current implementation we select a tier at random and then select a random item from that tier. This will produce skewed results in two likely usage scenarios: Tiers have substantially different numbers if items There are many items replicated across tiers In LSM we choose a random chunk, weighting by the number of item

The random cursor implementation for tiered cursors is quite simple. It picks a tier at random and picks a random element from it. If that tier is empty it tries again. The problem (as the code below shows) is that if all the tiers are empty it will never stop trying.

If we try a tier and get {{WTNOTFOUND}} we shouldn't try it again. Then if we run out of tiers (i.e., we get {{WTNOTFOUND}} from all of them), we know there is nothing in the table. We can do this by generating a random permutation of the tables and then trying the tables in that order.
Simplified the code to just pick a tier at random and then iterate over the tiers in order (wrapping around if needed) when it finds an empty tier.

To handle out of order timestamp, we will change the timestamps on the update chain. However, that should only be triggered for a committed update. If we write a prepared update to disk and its prepared timestamp is out of order, the current implementation will also trigger out of order timestamp handling, which is wrong as the prepared update can be aborted. This ticket is to fix this issue and write a test to ensure prepared updates should not trigger out of order timestamp handling.

We should investigate improvements to the WT cache eviction algorithm based on newer cache replacement algorithms. WiredTiger approximates a widely-used cache replacement algorithm—LRU with midpoint insertion—to provide scan resistance. I.e., to avoid the problem where a one-time scan of a large table causes everything else to be evicted in a standard LRU cache. In a traditional implementation, this works using a conventional LRU list. When when new data is added to the cache, it is inserted at

It's worth noting that WiredTiger attempts to approximate midpoint insertion by assigning an initial {{readgen}} that is half way between the current value and the oldest sampled value in cache (cf {{\wtcachereadgennew}}). That said, this code has not been touched or evaluated for at least 3 years to the best of my knowledge.

[~michael.cahill], thanks for the pointer. I (obviously) hadn't found that bit of the code. It's good to know that we do that. I'll update the description accordingly and frame this ticket as looking for improvements to the current implementation rather than suggesting we don't have a scan resistant cache.

FWIW: MySQL uses LIRS replacement. Postgres implemented ARC in the early 2000s, but replaced the code with the older, and less-adaptive, LRU-2Q over concerns about IBM patenting ARC. InnoDB uses midpoint insertion.

In WT-5479, when sweep is running frequently and closing handles it needs to acquire the dhandle lock for writing. When checkpoint is running in the gathering handles phase it holds the schema lock and needs to hold the dhandle lock for reading. Sweep can interfere with that checkpoint operation resulting in holding the schema lock longer. Since sweep is a background non-time critical operation, we should avoid grabbing that lock for writing if gathering handles is in progress.

The visibility rules of the entries in the history store will be defined in accordance with the visibility rules corresponding to the user sessions. There will be exceptions to this general rule to handle modify updates. This could be verified through testing.

Generally, only insert and delete operations will be performed on the history store. As the history store contains committed historical versions, update operation is not required to be performed on the history store. There are exceptions to this rule, but the update will happen only to the stop time pair of the entry. This could be asserted.
Only committed updates could be part of the history store, in any situation an uncommitted update could never be part of history store.

A particular historical version should be added to the history store only once. This could be verified by adding a diagnostic flag to the update structure and set it when it added to the history store. Assert can be added based on this flag to verify that an update is never added twice to the history store.

We do allow adding same history key [ {{btreeid,userkey,startts}} ] into history store again with a different {{hscounter}}. We already have a flag {{WTUPDATEHS}} that ensures that a user update is not added more than once to update list for history store table. Therefore, I used this ticket to add an another check that we do not add a new value that matches the existing value for the same [ {{btreeid,userkey,startts}} ] history store key.

There could be multiple historical versions associated with a single user-level key. Hence to maintain the uniqueness of keys in the history store, we need to have some other fields which will be part of the history store key along with the user key. Each and every historical version will form a unique key within the history store. An assert can be added in the insert function of the history store to check if a duplicate key is ever found.

Looking at the function {{hsinsertrecordwithbtree()}}, I believe [we are deliberately allowing duplicate history store keys| (which are combination of btree id, user key, and timestamp) to be stored by keeping track of a counter field. Essentially we can have history store keys with same btree id, user key and timestamp, which only differ based on a counter value to allow iterating over similar keys based on the order in which they were inserted into the history store. If durable timestamp is same as commit timestamp for any update, then no need to persist the durable timestamp for that update. We could save some space on disk.

Avoid writing the durable timestamp when the difference between commit and durable timestamp is zero for the value cell of both the start and stop timestamps. We write zero even for the address cell because it is very rare where the aggregated both commit and durable timestamps are the same. So instead of adding code to avoid writing zero is an overhead than the benefit for address cells.

For non-prepared transactions, both commit and durable timestamps are the same. Instead of saving both the values in the {{value}} cell, store only the commit timestamp and whenever the {{value}} cell is unpacked, make sure to set the durable timestamp also as commit timestamp for the cells that don't have a durable timestamp.

There is no error, and the false return value would be irrelevant to the caller. In fact the send method does not have to call flush at all; it just does so to make some effort to fill the kernel's TCP transmit buffer. It is up to the caller to call flush() either way, no matter what was or was not returned by doFlush(). JBoss Remoting in fact does this - when the send queue is empty, it calls flush until flush returns true to ensure that all data has been sent to the kernel for transmission.

The Descheduler operator should allow users to specify a specific PriorityClass name or value threshold above which no pod should be evicted. This will need to be an option exposed in the operator CRD which is either a string, integer, or both (the Descheduler can accept PriorityClass names or Priority values)

The Descheduler Operator should provide the ability to include/exclude certain namespaces to the user. It currently has hardcoded logic to exclude all namespaces prefixed with `openshift-` or `kube-`. Customers would like the ability to provide a similar pattern, or specific list. This would be difficult to implement on a per-profile basis without considerable refactoring of the operator CRD, so it should be implemented as a top-level option.

When you update an account in Sourcetree it resets both the git and REST credentials.
